planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; propagate vegetatively to keep the strain true, since seed-grown plants revert toward the generic commercial type.

directions: Suvasini is a university-released curry leaf selection from Karnataka, bred for noticeably faster, more vigorous growth and reduced winter sensitivity compared to older Indian strains such as Gamthi. Its paler green leaves carry a milder aroma than the darker, more pungent Gamthi type, making it a good choice for cooks who want a heavier, quicker harvest rather than the most intensely flavored leaf. Grow it exactly as you would standard curry leaf, in full sun and well-drained soil, and expect it to fill out a container or bed considerably faster than slower regional strains. Snip branch tips regularly to keep growth dense and productive, and mulch heavily or bring potted plants under cover whenever hard freezes threaten.
sources: International Society for Horticultural Science (ISHS) — Acta Horticulturae research on curry leaf cultivar 'Suvasini'

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade; this compact strain suits large patio containers as well as in-ground Gulf Coast beds.

directions: Gomati is a naturally dwarf, bushy curry leaf strain that stays far more compact than seed-grown commercial curry leaf while still producing an abundant, densely packed flush of small, intensely aromatic leaves. Its shrubbier, multi-branched habit and smaller ultimate size make it a better fit than standard curry leaf for raised beds, large pots, and smaller Gulf Coast gardens where a 6-10 foot tree is impractical. Grow it in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, and pinch tips regularly to keep the already-bushy habit dense. It flowers more readily than slower strains; remove flower clusters if maximum leaf production is the goal, and protect container plants from hard freezes in zone 9.

common_name: Thai Magic Basil (Wine-Red Ornamental Thai Basil)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger passes into warm, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Gulf Coast gardeners can resow through mid-summer for a continuous supply.

directions: Thai Magic is a decorative, robust Thai basil valued for unusually large, glossy, thick leaves and showy wine-red flower clusters that contrast strongly with the dark green foliage, making it as ornamental as it is useful in the kitchen. Its flavor is milder and sweeter than standard Thai basil, with the same anise-licorice backnote but less of the clove-like sharpness found in cultivars like Siam Queen. The dense, bushy plants hold up well to Gulf Coast heat and humidity and keep producing new leaves if flower spikes are pinched out regularly. Harvest by cutting stem tips just above a leaf pair to encourage continued branching, and expect vigorous regrowth through the entire warm season.
sources: Mill Creek Plants — Basil, Thai Magic
Hazzard's Greenhouse — Basil Thai Magic seed listing

common_name: Kapoori Betel Leaf (Soft Aromatic South Indian Paan Leaf)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in partial shade in moist, humus-rich soil with a support for climbing; give it the same warm, humid, filtered-light conditions as common betel vine.

directions: Kapoori is a widely grown South Indian type of betel leaf, distinguished from coarser betel leaf types by its thinner, narrower, more elliptical leaves with a soft texture and a notably fragrant, refreshing aroma favored for fresh chewing preparations. It is grown the same way as the common betel vine, climbing by node roots up a trellis or trunk in warm, humid, partially shaded conditions, and dislikes both full sun and dry soil. In Gulf Coast gardens treat it as a protected perennial vine in the warmest coastal zones or as a container plant brought indoors before cold weather elsewhere. Harvest individual leaves as needed once the vine is established, and keep soil evenly moist without letting it become waterlogged.
sources: Journal of Pharmacognosy and Phytochemistry — betel leaf (Piper betle) variety characterization
